pages.name: In step
pages.task: A mass on a spring swings on its own at 2 Hz. A push that comes and goes drives it. Which push gives the biggest steady swing?
pages.why: The mass swings on its own at 2 Hz. A push at 2 Hz arrives in step, once each swing. So each push adds to the swing. It grows until damping takes out as much as each push puts in. That is [[resonance]].

pages.name: The heavy spot's pull
pages.text: A rotor with more mass on one side has an [[unbalance]]. Here an example 20 g heavy spot sits 0.15 m from the axis. The shaft must pull it round. So the spot pulls the shaft outwards just as hard. That pull is the spot's mass × its radius × the angular speed squared, with the speed in rad/s. It points at the spot and turns with it. Its up-and-down part pushes the mounts up, then down, once a turn. At 1450 rev/min the pull is 69 N.

pages.name: Twice the speed
pages.task: At 1450 rev/min the heavy spot pulls with 69 N. What does it pull with at 2900 rev/min?
pages.why: 2900 rev/min is twice 1450. At double the speed, the spot moves twice as fast and swings its direction round twice as quickly. So the pull is four times as big. At 303.7 rad/s it is 0.02 × 0.15 × 303.7² = 277 N.

pages.name: The critical speed
pages.text: The shake does not just grow with speed. The rotor swings on its own at √(stiffness ÷ mass) = √(500,000 ÷ 50) = 100 rad/s. That is its [[natural frequency]], 100 ÷ 2π = 15.9 times a second. At 955 rev/min it turns that often. Each push then arrives in step and adds to the swing. That is the [[critical speed]]. Above it, each push reverses before the rotor can follow. It spins about its centre of mass, 0.003 kg m ÷ 50 kg = 0.06 mm off the shaft's line. So the shake settles near 0.06 mm.
pages.alt: A disc on a shaft, seen end on, turns at 2400 revolutions a minute on springy mounts. An arrow from its axis shows the heavy spot's pull. Below, a graph of shake against speed fills in dot by dot as the speed sweeps.

pages.name: Where it peaks
pages.task: A pump set's mounts swing on their own at 20 Hz. The pump runs up to 2900 rev/min. At what speed does it shake hardest on the way up?
pages.why: The shake peaks where the shaft turns as often as the mounts swing: 20 times a second. That is 20 × 60 = 1200 turns a minute, the pump's [[critical speed]]. Above it, the shake falls back.

pages.name: Damping
pages.text: [[Damping]] takes energy out of every swing. A damping factor of 1 is critical damping: a nudged mass settles without swinging. So 0.05 is light. At the critical speed the spring and the rotor's inertia cancel. Only damping holds back the pull. So the peak is 0.06 mm ÷ (2 × the damping factor). Here it rises from 0.05 to 0.2. The peak drops from 0.6 mm to about 0.15 mm and spreads wider. Elsewhere the shake hardly changes. At 0.02 the peak climbs to 1.5 mm.
pages.alt: A disc on a shaft, seen end on, turns at 955 revolutions a minute on springy mounts. An arrow from its axis shows the heavy spot's pull. Below, a graph of shake against speed.

pages.name: Double the damping
pages.task: At a damping factor of 0.05 this rotor shakes 0.6 mm at its critical speed. The damping doubles to 0.1. How far does it shake at the critical speed now?
pages.why: At the critical speed the shake is 0.06 mm ÷ (2 × the damping factor). At 0.1 that is 0.06 ÷ 0.2 = 0.3 mm. Doubling the damping halves the peak. The pull is still there.
pages.alt: A graph of shake against speed for damping 0.05, peaking at 0.6 millimetres at the critical speed.

pages.name: A balance weight
pages.text: Balancing removes the cause that damping only softens. A 20 g [[balance weight]] sits 0.15 m out, like the spot. At any speed its pull is just as big, and points at the weight. The two pulls add, as forces do. Beside the spot, the total pull is twice as big. A quarter turn away, it is 1.41 times as big. Opposite the spot, the two pulls cancel at every speed. The curve goes flat at zero.
pages.alt: A disc on a shaft, seen end on, turns at 1450 revolutions a minute on springy mounts. An arrow from its axis shows the heavy spot's pull, a second the balance weight's pull and a third their total. Below, a graph of shake against speed.

pages.name: Balance mass
pages.task: A rotor has a 30 g heavy spot 0.10 m from its axis. A balance weight goes opposite, 0.15 m out. What mass must it have?
pages.why: The weight needs the same mass × radius as the spot: 30 g × 0.10 m = 3 g m. At 0.15 m that takes 3 g m ÷ 0.15 m = 20 g. Then their pulls are equal and opposite at every speed.

pages.name: A long rotor
pages.text: A long rotor needs more care. Here a 20 g heavy spot sits near each end, on opposite sides. Their two pulls cancel in total. But one pushes its end up while the other pushes the far end down. So together they rock the shaft end over end, as a [[couple]]. A balance weight at each end, opposite each spot, stops the rocking. A flexible rotor needs weights in more places.

pages.name: A shake on the way up
pages.task: A motor runs up to 1450 rev/min. It shakes hard for a moment near 950 rev/min, then runs smoothly. Why?
pages.answer: It passes through a critical speed
pages.why: Near 950 rev/min the motor turns as often as its mounts swing on their own. Each turn's push arrives in step, so the shake builds. Past that [[critical speed]], each push reverses before the motor can follow. So it runs smoothly at 1450 rev/min.

pages.name: Pull at speed
pages.task: A 10 g heavy spot sits 0.2 m from the axis. The rotor turns at 3000 rev/min. How hard does the spot pull on the shaft?
pages.why: First change the speed to rad/s: 3000 × 2π ÷ 60 = 314.2 rad/s. The pull is the mass × the radius × the speed squared: 0.01 × 0.2 × 314.2² = 197 N.

pages.name: Stiffer mounts
pages.task: The 50 kg rotor's mounts are stiffened from 500 to 2000 kN/m. Where is its critical speed now?
pages.why: The mounts swing on their own at √(stiffness ÷ mass) rad/s. Four times the stiffness gives √4 = 2 times that. So √(2,000,000 ÷ 50) = 200 rad/s, which is 200 × 60 ÷ 2π = 1910 rev/min. A heavier rotor does the opposite: more mass lowers it.

pages.name: What builds on this
pages.text: Two more ideas build on moments and stress. A beam bends under a load. A shaft twists a little as it carries torque. Both start from what you have used here: moments, stress and strain.
